title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance (Unified ADR)
author: Elena Park
body:
Summary
-------
This document captures Redwood Inference's unified architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure/IaC, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also records the associated ADRs (decisions, context, alternatives) for cross-team alignment. The intended audience is engineering, platform, SRE, and product teams delivering services and model-serving integrations.

Goals
-----
- Provide a single source of truth that reduces design drift between teams.
- Set measurable SLOs and observability requirements for all externally-facing and internal services.
- Standardize API shapes and versioning to make client integrations predictable.
- Enforce infra patterns that enable reproducible deployments across Hosted/Dedicated/Private modes.
- Define model-serving standards that protect quality and cost objectives.

Scope
-----
Applies to: Redwood API services, serving runtime components, platform control plane, customer-facing internal tools, and new microservices built after 2025-06. Exceptions must be documented and approved by the architecture board.

1) API Standards
----------------
Purpose: Ensure consistency, discoverability, and backwards-compatible evolution of public and internal HTTP/GRPC APIs.

High-level rules:
- Use REST/JSON for public-facing HTTP endpoints; gRPC is allowed for high-throughput internal service-to-service RPCs.
- All public APIs must implement stable, documented OpenAPI v3 specs stored in the api-specs repo.
- Versioning: Use semantic URI versioning (/v1/, /v2/). Deprecation windows: minimum 90 days for public APIs; 30 days for internal APIs with deprecation warnings in logs and metrics.
- Error model: consistent envelope {"code": string, "message": string, "details": optional object}. HTTP status mapping documented: 4xx = client, 5xx = server.
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination for long result sets. Avoid offset-based for large datasets.
- Idempotency: All mutating endpoints must accept Idempotency-Key header and persist idempotency entries for 24 hours.
- Rate limiting: Accept and return standard headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset).

Design guidelines and examples:
- Use nouns for resources: POST /v1/deployments, GET /v1/models/{model_id}/metrics
- Avoid RPC-style verbs in paths: prefer /jobs instead of /runJob.
- Use HTTP 202 for long-running operations and provide operation resource (/v1/operations/{op_id}) to poll or subscribe for updates.

OpenAPI & contract testing:
- Every public API must have OpenAPI spec committed in api-specs and a CI job that runs contract tests against a staging mock. Failures block merge.

API Security:
- Public API keys scoped by route; require AAA checks in gateway. Sensitive routes require token rotation and short-lived tokens by default.

2) Coding Standards
--------------------
Purpose: Maintain readability, reduce defects, and make on-call transitions easier.

Languages in active use: Go (backend services, runtime control plane), Python (evals, SDKs), TypeScript (console & SDKs), Rust/C++ (performance-critical kernels).

General rules:
- Follow language-specific style guides: Go: effective go + golangci-lint; Python: PEP8 + black + pylint; TypeScript: ESLint + Prettier.
- Single source of truth for lint config in /repo-tools/configs. Projects must import these configs.
- Unit test coverage: minimum 60% for service logic; 80%+ encouraged for critical modules (auth, billing, routing).
- CI requirements: all PRs must pass unit tests, linters, and security scans. Merges blocked on failing checks.
- Code review: at least one approval from a sibling-team reviewer for infra or cross-cutting changes.
- Secrets: No secrets in code or git. Use vault-backed secret injection via deployment pipelines.

Performance-aware coding:
- Avoid synchronous blocking on high-latency IO in request paths. Prefer async or background work for non-critical tasks.
- Hot paths must include microbenchmarks and profiling annotations.

3) Infrastructure & IaC Standards
--------------------------------
Purpose: Ensure reproducible, auditable infrastructure across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Principles:
- All infra changes must be expressed in Terraform (monorepo: infra/terraform) or Helm charts for Kubernetes manifests. No manual console changes without documented approval and postmortem.
- Modules: Use standardized Terraform modules for networking, IAM, logging, and compute. Modules must be versioned and published with CHANGELOG.
- Environments: clear separation (dev, staging, prod); CI/CD pipelines must use environment-specific variable files stored in encrypted gitops repo.
- Drift detection: daily automated drift detection jobs that create paged tickets for unresolved drift.

Networking & security:
- VPC per customer for Private deployments or per-cluster isolation for Dedicated. Default deny security groups with least privilege inbound/outbound rules.
- KMS-backed encryption for all at-rest secrets and customer data. HSM option for high-compliance customers.

Capacity & autoscaling:
- GPU fleet runs on dedicated pools; terraform variable driven autoscaling policies. Scaling based on queue length and p95 token-latency forecasts.
- Burst capacity for Dedicated customers is allowed with explicit billing alerting.

4) Model-Serving Standards
--------------------------
Purpose: Deliver predictable latency, cost, and quality for model inference across different deployment modes.

Model packaging and onboarding:
- Models must include a manifest (model.manifest.json) with fields: model_id, architecture, quantization_profile, expected_input_shape, max_context, owner, and a list of tests with baseline metrics.
- Acceptable formats: ONNX, TorchScript, and internal optimized formats. Provide conversion steps in model-onboarding playbook.
- CI for models: onboarding CI runs sample inference, unit eval prompts, and quantization checks. Failure blocks rollout.

Serving runtime contracts:
- Runtime must expose adaptors implementing the inference contract: predict(request) -> streaming/chunked responses, with backpressure signals.
- KV cache contract: runtimes must expose cache hit/miss metrics and allow prefix caching with TTLs configurable per-model.
- Quantized model policy: prefer int8 or int4 quantization for non-LLM-critical flows; maintain at least one FP16/FP32 canonical variant for quality-sensitive customers.

Rollout & compatibility:
- Canary rollout by traffic % with automatic rollback on defined quality regressions (see Quality Guardrails doc).
- Model variant compatibility: runtime should be able to fallback to a compatible variant when the canonical model is unavailable. Compatibility matrix stored in model-catalog.

Operational controls:
- Maximum allowed sequence length is a runtime config per-route; requests exceeding it must be rejected with descriptive error and a Redirect-to-truncation strategy.
- Per-customer rate & concurrency limits enforced at gateway and runtime.

5) Observability Standards
--------------------------
Purpose: Provide actionable telemetry for debugging, capacity planning, and SLO reporting.

Metrics (minimum required)
- API gateway: request_count, request_errors, request_duration_seconds (histogram/p99), auth_failures.
- Runtime/model-serving: tokens_generated_total, token_generation_latency_seconds (p50/p95/p99), kv_cache_hits_total, kv_cache_misses_total, gpu_utilization, host_mem_pressure_percent.
- Infrastructure: instance_up, container_restarts_total, disk_io_latency_seconds, network_out_bytes_total.

SLO & alerting thresholds
- User-facing generation endpoints: p99 latency <= 500ms for short-context (<=512 tokens) requests, error rate < 0.5% (5xx filtered).
- SDK/backend control plane APIs: p99 <= 200ms, error rate < 0.2%.
- GPU pool utilization: target 60-80% steady-state; alert on sustained >90% for 10m.
- KV cache hit-rate objective: >= 70% for workloads with known prefix reuse.

Tracing & logs
- Distributed tracing: propagate traceparent for every request. Capture spans for gateway, router, runtime, and model invocation. Sample 10% by default; error traces always captured.
- Logs must include structured JSON with keys: timestamp, level, service, trace_id, span_id, request_id, msg, attrs. PII must never be logged.

Dashboards and ownership
- Each service must publish three dashboards: Overview (latency/error/throughput), Capacity (utilization, queue depth), and SLOs (error budget burn). Owners must be declared in service metadata.

6) Performance Standards & Benchmarks
------------------------------------
Purpose: Keep latency and cost predictability as core product differentiators.

Benchmarking practice:
- All public model+runtime pairs must have published perf profiles: tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies at 512-token and 2048-token contexts. Profiles stored in benchmarking-and-perf-suite.
- Microbenchmarks required for kernel changes; macrobenchmarks required before model upgrades.

Performance targets (examples):
- Hosted API (small models): p99 <= 200ms for <=512 tokens.
- Serving runtime (medium LLMs): throughput >= 120 tokens/sec per A100-equivalent device under typical batching.
- Embeddings endpoints: median embedding latency <= 50ms for typical sized inputs (<=128 tokens).

Cost-aware controls:
- Default deployment templates include batching configs, prefix caching enabled, and recommended quantization. Engineers must include a cost impact assessment for changes that increase per-token compute by >10%.

7) Decision Records (ADRs)
--------------------------
This section records the major architectural decisions and alternatives considered. Each ADR includes: id, title, status, date, context, decision, consequences, and links to implementation work. ADRs should be stored under architecture/adrs with a short summary in this doc.

ADR-2026-01: API Versioning Model (published 2026-01-15)
- Decision: URI-based versioning (/vN/) for public APIs, feature flags for minor compat changes.
- Rationale: Simplicity for clients and clear gateway routing rules.
- Consequence: Requires stricter deprecation policy and toolchain support for migrating clients.

ADR-2026-02: Runtime Language Choice for Hot Path
- Decision: Keep GPU kernels in C++/CUDA, control plane in Go.
- Rationale: Performance and observability trade-offs.
- Consequence: Cross-language integration pattern and interface contract required (gRPC + well-defined adapters).

ADR-2026-03: Model Quantization Strategy
- Decision: Default to int8 for cost-sensitive workloads; require baseline FP16 test for quality-sensitive customers.
- Rationale: Significant cost savings while controlling quality regressions.
- Consequence: Need for automated quantization CI and storing canonical FP16 variants.

Process for new ADRs
1. Draft ADR in ADR template (architecture-and-standards/adrs).
2. Reviewers: at least architecture board + impacted service owners.
3. Publish in this doc and archive in adrs/ with cross-links.

Implementation checklist (mandatory for infra and runtime changes)
- Design doc with owner, expected impact, rollback plan.
- Perf & correctness test plan, including representative workloads.
- Observability additions (metrics, traces, logs) instrumented and dashboarded.
- Security review and data classification sign-off if customer data touched.

Rollout & Change Management
--------------------------
- All changes to production must follow change-management playbook: change ticket, planned maintenance window if required, progressive rollout (canary -> ramp -> full).
- Emergency changes require postmortem within 72 hours.

Appendices
---------
A. Sample OpenAPI snippet
{
  "paths": {
    "/v1/generate": {
      "post": {
        "summary": "Synchronous text generation",
        "requestBody": {"content": {"application/json": {}}},
        "responses": {"200": {"description": "OK"}}
      }
    }
  }
}

B. Model manifest example (model.manifest.json)
{
  "model_id": "redwood/llama-13b-v2",
  "architecture": "decoder-only",
  "quantization_profile": "int8-optimized-v1",
  "expected_input_shape": [1, 2048],
  "max_context": "2048",
  "owner": "applied-ml",
  "tests": ["basic-inference", "eval-promptset-x" ]
}

C. Operational runbook excerpt: rollback on perf regression
1. Detect: alert when model p99 latency increases >30% vs baseline for 10m.
2. Runbook steps:
   a. Escalate to runtime-owner and ML-owner.
   b. Halt new deployments for the model.
   c. Trigger automatic rollback to previous variant if enabled.
   d. If rollback fails, route traffic to fallback compatible variant or a smaller model.
   e. Open incident and attach perf traces and sample requests.

D. Ownership matrix (text table)
- Service owners must be declared in service metadata and updated in group-directory. Example: runtime-service -> owner: eng-serving-runtime, oncall: eng-sre.

E. Related docs
- model-onboarding, quality-guardrails, observability-standards, infra-standards, api-standards.

Contact and feedback
--------------------
For questions or suggested changes, open an architecture request ticket and add the architecture-board label. Primary document owner: Elena Park (eng-architecture).
